spans.t: This is a small, quiet book for eight days. It is made to go with the Camino de Invierno, the Winter Way, which the app lists as running from Ponferrada to Santiago de Compostela, about 260 km.
Invierno
is the Spanish word for winter. The name belongs to the road, and you can read the book in any season, on the road or at home.

The app's own route notes call it a road with few pilgrims, and they advise planning where you will sleep ahead. That is worth knowing here. A quiet road gives you long hours alone, and some evenings in a village where you may be the only walker at the table. This book is made for those hours. It is quiet and consoling, and it does not talk much. It keeps you company and lets you get on.
A day
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
The morning
has three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
Revelations of Divine Love

, a book written in English in the fourteenth century by Julian of Norwich. The words are exactly as they stand in the 1901 edition we use, old forms and all. Read the passage twice, the second time aloud if you can, or under your breath. Old English slows the eye, and that is half of its use.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Julian's. It begins with something from the road, a coat, a head torch, a door, and lets the passage open it. It says plainly what the passage says. It says where the passage is hard, and it is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour, and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. You will not need a notebook. Most of them are better done on your feet.

spans.t: The evening
has two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.

A look back over the day with the morning's passage in mind. It names what may have been hard and what may have been good, and it ends with two or three gentle questions. You do not have to answer them in writing. They are for lying down with.
A short prayer.
Original, and short. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular.

spans.t: A Christian book, and who it is for

Julian was a Christian of the fourteenth century, and she writes as one. She speaks of God, of Christ, of the Church and of sin in her own medieval terms, and she hopes that her readers will take them as she does. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All are welcome here. You do not need to share her belief to recognise what she noticed about being small, being held, being afraid, and being tired. Where she is hard to follow, we say so.
The shape of the eight days
The days follow a walk. They do not follow the order of her book.

items.t: Day 1.
The smallness of things.
Day 2.
Being held.
Day 3.
The courtesy of God.
Day 4.
Sin and suffering, told honestly.
Day 5.
"All shall be well".
Day 6.
The way of prayer.
Day 7.
The long patience.
Day 8.
The end, and the beginning.

spans.t: At an ordinary pace of 20 to 25 km a day, about 260 km is roughly two weeks, give or take. Eight days will not match every day of such a walk, and they do not need to. Read a day when it suits you: on a rest day, on a day of rain, on a day when the road is hard. Repeat one that helped. Read two at once if you want. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last of all, when the boots are off. At home it works the same way: the morning with your tea, the evening before bed.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, sometimes with a shared kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well. Julian's own words are explained where they first come up. She says
shewing
for what we would call a vision, and
homely
for something close to "at home".
Read slowly. The book was made to be read a few lines at a time.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The woman
Revelations of Divine Love

was written by Julian, an anchoress at Norwich. The edition we use says so on its title page. An anchoress was a woman who had chosen to live shut in a small room built against a church, given over to prayer. The introduction to the edition describes such rooms as having a window into the church, so that she could follow its services, and another opening to the outside world, where people who wished to speak with her could come.

Very little is known about her outer life, and we will not pretend otherwise. She does not give her name in the book. An old note quoted in the edition says that her name was Julian and that she was a recluse at Norwich. She calls herself
a simple creature unlettered
. From her own words the edition's editor works out that she was born about 1342, since Julian says she was
thirty years old and a half

in May 1373. We do not know when she died. The edition quotes an old note that has her still living in 1442. Modern accounts usually place her last record at about 1416, and we have not tried to settle it.
The book

Julian says that her showings came to her on the thirteenth of May, 1373. She was gravely ill and thought she was dying. She tells us that fifteen showings lasted from about four o'clock in the morning until after nine, and that a sixteenth followed the next night. She wrote the book in English, and she says that
fifteen years after, and more
she was answered as to what they meant. The edition's introduction reckons from her words that the book cannot have been finished before about 1393.

In this edition the book has 86 short chapters. Most of it concerns the suffering of Christ, which she saw in visions and describes plainly. Around that centre she writes about sin, about the Church, about prayer, and about a comfort she believed was meant for everyone:
we are all one in comfort
, she says. She also says, early on, that in all things she believes
as Holy Church believeth, preacheth, and teacheth
. She was a fourteenth-century Christian, and the book is built that way.
Why it suits a pilgrim

Julian says little about roads. Yet the book is made of things a walker meets: a small round thing in the palm of the hand, the clothes you wear, a great lord and a poor servant, a child that has fallen and runs to its mother, a light in the night. It is a quiet book, and its theme, as the edition's introduction puts it, is comfort.

It is also hard in places, and we have chosen with that in mind. She writes in the terms of her Church, with sin, penance, hell and the Fiend all on the page. The passages here are the ones a general reader can follow, and the reflections say where she is difficult. We have not tried to explain doctrine to anyone who did not ask, and we have left aside the long chapters on the Passion. She says that as truly as God is our Father, God is our Mother (chapter 59, and on to chapter 63). We have not chosen a passage for that, but you will meet it if you read on.
The edition, and what we did with it
The English in the passages is from
Revelations of Divine Love
, in the edition of Grace Warrack, published in London in 1901. The title page calls it
A version from the MS. in the British Museum

. The edition's own notes tell us what that means. Julian's English book survives in two manuscripts, one in Paris from the sixteenth century and one in the British Museum, in seventeenth-century handwriting, called the Sloane manuscript. The editor transcribed the Sloane manuscript. She divided it into paragraphs, added capital letters, varied the punctuation, and, to make a book for general use, adopted modern spelling and put most words no longer in use into modern English. A few old words she kept for their charm or their meaning, and she almost always left the old forms of grammar as they were. She says that her rule was never to omit a word of the manuscript, and that the few words she added are in square brackets.

That is what the edition says of itself. We have not seen the manuscripts. What we use is a modernised text, not Julian's fourteenth-century English, and we take the editor's word for how closely it follows the manuscript. Scholars today also know a shorter account of the same showings. It was not known when this edition was made, and it is not used here.

The edition is in the public domain, and the text is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 52958. Every quotation in this book was checked against it, word for word. We quote only Julian's own text, never the editor's introduction, notes or glossary.
What we changed in the passages is nothing in the words. We kept the old spellings,
shewed
and
hazel-nut
and
all-thing

, and the editor's square brackets, where she added a word. We left out the small footnote numbers. A mark like this, …, shows a gap between two stretches. In three passages, on Days 2, 5 and 6, the mark falls in the middle of a sentence. That is where the edition printed a footnote number, and nothing of Julian's is missing there. The choice of the eight passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and they are original. The eight passages come from eleven of her chapters: 5, 6, 7, 27, 29, 31, 32, 41, 77, 83 and 86.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.

chapters.title: Day 1. The size of a hazelnut

spans.t: What looks enormous this morning, and what is holding it?
The passage

paras.t: Also in this He shewed me a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball. I looked thereupon with eye of my understanding, and thought:
What may this be?
And it was answered generally thus:
it is all that is made.
I marvelled how it might last, for methought it might suddenly have fallen to naught for little[ness]. And I was answered in my understanding:
It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it.

And so All-thing hath the Being by the love of God. In this Little Thing I saw three properties. The first is that God made it, the second is that God loveth it, the third, that God keepeth it. … For this is the cause why we be not all in ease of heart and soul: that we seek here rest in those things that are so little, wherein is no rest, and know not our God that is All-mighty, All-wise, All-good. For He is the Very Rest. God willeth to be known, and it pleaseth Him that we rest in Him; for all that is beneath Him sufficeth not us.

spans.t: Reflection

At the start of a long walk the road is too big to think about. You know the number, about 260 km, and the number does nothing for you. It stands in the mind like a wall. The only way through is to stop looking at the whole of it and look at the next bend, the next waymark, the ground under your boots.

Julian of Norwich was shown a different kind of smallness. She was gravely ill and believed she was dying when she saw it: lying in the palm of her hand, a little thing the size of a hazelnut, round as a ball. She looked at it and asked what it could be. The answer was that it is all that is made. The whole of creation, small enough to hold.

Her next thought is the one that matters. She marvelled that it could last at all. It looked as though it might drop into nothing at any moment, for being so little. And the answer she was given is the heart of the passage: it lasts, and always will, because God loves it.
Then she names three things she saw in it, short enough to carry in a pocket. God made it. God loves it. God keeps it. Made, loved, kept.

Notice what she does not say. She does not say that the world is nothing, or that it does not matter. She says it is small, and held, and the two belong together. A little later she explains why it looked so small to her: she was seeing it in the presence of its Maker, and
all that is made seemeth full little
to a soul that sees that. It is a matter of where you are standing.

Anyone who has climbed a hill on the way will know the effect. The village you left an hour ago, which seemed to fill the whole of yesterday evening, becomes a few roofs in a fold of land. The valley you were dreading is a pale stripe on the ground. Nothing has changed except your height.

So much for the gentle part. Here is the hard one. In the same chapter Julian says that we need to hold all that is made as nought, her word, if we are to love God, and that we are never at ease because we look for rest in things too small to give it. Read cold, that sounds like contempt for the world: for houses, for people, for a good lunch. It cannot mean that, if what she has just been shown is true. The small thing lasts because it is loved. Her "nought" has to do with where you put your weight. Walkers know something about weight. A pack is full of good things, and none of them is a place to lean.

Read generously, she is saying that nothing made is big enough to be the place where the heart finally rests. That is not an insult to the things. It is a description of the heart. The passage names the cure for restlessness as
the Very Rest

, and it says that everything below that falls short of us. You may or may not take the name she gives it. The restlessness itself is hard to deny, and a road is a good place to notice it: the wish to be there already, wherever there is.

Set an honest doubt beside this. It is easy to say that all is small and held on a morning when your legs are fresh. The things that really trouble you do not feel the size of a nut. A worry about home, a knee, a decision waiting at work: it fills the sky. Julian does not argue with that, and nor should this page. She does not say that your worry is small. She says that what holds it is not.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Something small, in keeping. To look, once, at one little thing, a stone or a seed head or a button, and let it be made, loved and kept. To notice that the long road is only ever walked a step at a time, and that you are walking this one. And, if you can, to lean a little less on what was never built to bear you, and a little more on what, in her sight, was holding the nut.
For the walk

items.t: What looks enormous to me this morning, and what is it like to see it from a little higher up?

Find one small thing on the path, a pebble or a leaf or a fallen nut, and hold it in your open palm for a minute. Feel its weight and say, in your own words, made, loved, kept. Then put it back where you found it, and walk on a little lighter.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The boots are off. Your feet are somewhere between sore and grateful, and the day, which this morning was 260 km of road, has at last turned out to be exactly as long as today. That is a small piece of news, and it is worth a minute before you do anything else.

Look back at what seemed huge at breakfast. Some of it will have shrunk without your noticing. The long climb is behind you, and it was a climb. The hill you dreaded took an hour and a half and a few songs you did not know you remembered. Some of it will not have shrunk. A worry can follow you for twenty kilometres and be exactly as big at six as it was at seven. That is allowed too. Nothing in Julian asks you to pretend that it dwindled.

Think now of the small things that were good. A drink of water that tasted of something. A cat on a wall. A gate that opened easily. The hour when the weather made up its mind. The people you passed, and the one who nodded. On a quiet road there may have been long stretches with no one at all, and if so, the quiet was a day-sized thing too, to be taken as it came.

Hold the three words once more. Made: this day, and the one who walked it. Loved: and not for how far you went. Kept: tonight, in a bed or on a bench, with the lights going out. You do not need to feel it. Julian says it lasts, whether or not anyone is watching how.
If you are too tired for any of this, that is the most natural thing in the world. Read the prayer, and sleep.

items.t: What looked enormous this morning, and how big was it by evening?
Which small thing did I notice today that I would have walked past at home?
Where could I rest my weight tonight, instead of holding it all up myself?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight the world is the size of this room. Thank you for what was made, and for whatever keeps it. Let the day be as long as it was and no longer. Hold what I cannot carry. Let me sleep like something small and safe.
What is wrapped around you that you did not make?
The passage

paras.t: For He hath no despite of that He hath made, nor hath He any disdain to serve us at the simplest office that to our body belongeth in nature, for love of the soul that He hath made to His own likeness. … For as the body is clad in the cloth, and the flesh in the skin, and the bones in the flesh, and the heart in the whole, … so are we, soul and body, clad in the Goodness of God, and enclosed. Yea, and more homely: for all these may waste and wear away, but the Goodness of God is ever whole; and more near to us, without any likeness; for truly our Lover desireth that our soul cleave to Him with all its might, and that we be ever-more cleaving to His Goodness.

spans.t: Reflection

Getting dressed on a walking morning is a small ceremony of layers. The thin one against the skin, then the shirt, then the warm one, then whatever keeps off the weather. Each layer has a job, and each one holds in the warmth of the one beneath. By the time the pack goes on you are wrapped in a sequence, and you do not think about it at all, until the day that one layer is missing.

Julian saw something very like this, and she put it into a sentence you can almost feel on your shoulders. The body is clad in cloth, the flesh in skin, the bones in flesh, the heart in the whole. Then comes the turn: so are we, soul and body, clad in the Goodness of God, and enclosed.
She does not stop at comfort, though. She says
more homely

, and she gives the reason: all those other coverings wear away. Cloth frays. Boots lose their soles. Skin cracks in the cold. The Goodness she means does not wear, because it is ever whole. Anyone who has watched a favourite jacket give out somewhere along the way will see the point. Everything you are wearing is on its way to being worn out. The covering she describes is not.
Before the cloth, though, there is a sentence that is easy to skim and worth a second look. God has no despite of what He has made, she writes, and no disdain
to serve us at the simplest office that to our body belongeth in nature

. The plainest needs of the body are not beneath notice. That is a surprising thing to find in a medieval book, and it is a comfort for a walker. Your feet, your hunger, your thirst, your need for a bed and a warm drink are not a distraction from the serious business. They are not too small to be held.

Now for the hard places. The word "enclosed" is the first. A person who walks for the sky, the long view and the open road may not love the word. Being enclosed can sound like being shut in. Julian means the opposite of a cage: the way a body is enclosed in its own warmth, the way a child is enclosed in an arm. But if the word jars, say so, and read it as held.
The second hard place is a bigger one. To be held is not the same as being spared. Julian was gravely ill when this was shown to her. A few chapters on, she writes that God
keepeth us even alike secure in woe and in weal

. She does not promise that the rain will stay off. The wrapping is not a roof. She says that you are kept in the rain, and in the sun, in equal measure, and she does not explain how. If that sounds thin, it is allowed to sound thin. She was not writing it from comfort.

And there is the plain difficulty of being held at all. Most people who walk a long road like to feel capable. You carry your own pack. You choose your own pace. To think of yourself as clad and carried, with little part in it, can feel like a loss of dignity. Notice that nothing in the passage asks you to do anything. The body does not dress itself in its skin. It is simply in it. The only thing left for you is to notice.

So what does it ask of an ordinary day? To pay attention, for a moment, to the layers. To feel the weight of a coat you did not weave, on a road other people made, past fields other people kept, towards a bed that someone made up. Almost nothing in your day was made by you alone. That is not an accusation. It is another way of saying that you are wrapped up in a good deal more than you can see.
Julian calls God
our Lover
, as freely as she says
Lord

. If you read that as an old word for someone who loves, it is not strange: someone whose whole wish is that you cleave to the good, and stay close to it. Take as much of that as is useful this morning. The cloth, at any rate, is yours to feel.
For the walk

items.t: What is wrapped around me this morning that I did not make?

At the first rest, when you put a layer on or take one off, pause with it in your hands. Name the sequence slowly, cloth, skin, flesh, bone, heart, and rest a hand on your chest on the last one. Then put the layer on, and notice that it was already warm.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Nobody at the end of a long walk wants a lecture, but a blanket is another matter. Wherever you sleep tonight, there is probably one: a rough grey wool one, a sleeping bag, a duvet that smells of someone else's washing powder. The bed does not ask whether you earned it. It takes your weight.

Think back over the day and ask where you were held. It need not be grand. A wall that you leaned on for five minutes. A bench someone put there. A set of waymarks that carried you through a place you could not have found. A stranger's directions. The fact that your legs went on working when you stopped asking them to. These are the cloth, and the skin, and the flesh.

Ask also where you tried to hold everything up yourself. Perhaps you spent an hour carrying a worry as if the road depended on it. Perhaps you walked too fast to prove something. There is a certain kind of tiredness that comes less from the kilometres than from the effort of being the only support. Julian would not say that you were wrong to try. She says only that the support was there, and did not wear.

Be honest, too, about the day's cold spots. Some part of today may have felt unwrapped: a long wet stretch, a loneliness at four in the afternoon, a message that landed badly. Being held, in her sense, did not make those hours easy. It does not have to be proved tonight. If the day did not feel held, you can leave the sentence unsaid and read the prayer as a wish.
And if the day did feel safe, let it. A good day does not need a reason.
Three questions for the warm dark:

items.t: Where today did I let something hold me, a wall, a stranger, a roof?
What was I carrying alone that I could have set down?
What, tonight, is simply keeping me warm?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I am wrapped in more than I made. Thank you for the cloth and the roof and the hands behind them. Hold me in the rain as in the sun. Let what wears out wear out gently. Let me be warm enough to rest.
Who has stooped to your level on this road, and who have you stooped to meet?
The passage

paras.t: And of all the sight it was most comfort to me that our God and Lord that is so reverend and dreadful, is so homely and courteous: and this most fulfilled me with comfort and assuredness of soul. … It is the most worship that a solemn King or a great Lord may do a poor servant if he will be homely with him, and specially if he sheweth it
himself
, of a full true meaning, and with a glad cheer, both privately and in company. Then thinketh this poor creature thus:

And what might this noble Lord do of more worship and joy to me than to shew me that am so simple this marvellous homeliness? Soothly it is more joy and pleasance to me than [if] he gave me great gifts and were himself strange in manner.

… For our courteous Lord willeth that we should be as homely with Him as heart may think or soul may desire. But [let us] beware that we take not so recklessly this homeliness as to leave courtesy. For our Lord Himself is sovereign homeliness, and as homely as He is, so courteous He is: for He is very courteous.

spans.t: Reflection

Think of a door at the end of a long afternoon. It is a plain door, in a village you have never seen, and behind it is someone whose job, or whose habit, is to take in strangers. Within a minute the whole day is rearranged. You are asked your name. A glass of water appears. You are shown where the bed is, where the boots go, where the kettle lives. You came in as a tired stranger and in the space of a few sentences you are a guest.
What matters about that minute is not the water. It is the manner. Someone with a house and a say in it has decided, for no reason except kindness, to treat you as one of the household.

Julian had been looking at something dreadful, in the old sense of the word: a vision so overwhelming that she calls it both horrifying and sweet. And out of the whole sight, she says, the most comfort was this: that God, who is so
reverend and dreadful
, is also
homely and courteous
. "Homely", in her English, means at home, familiar, one of the house. "Courteous" means gracious and gently considerate.

Then she gives an example, and it is a good one. A great lord, she says, can do no higher honour to a poor servant than to be homely with him, and above all to do it himself, with a true meaning and a glad face, in private and in company. The servant's thought is the part worth stopping at. What more could this noble lord do to honour me than to show me, so simple as I am, this marvellous homeliness? It is more joy than a heap of gifts would be, if he stayed distant in his manner.

You can feel the difference between a gift and a welcome. A cold parcel left on a step is a gift. A person who sits down opposite you with the same soup is something else. On a long road you may meet both, and you will know which one you are carrying home.

The next part is easy to miss, and it is the courtesy. Julian, who has just said how close and easy God can be, adds a check: beware that we take this homeliness so recklessly as to leave courtesy. As homely as He is, she says, so courteous He is. Nearness and good manners come together. Anyone who has stayed in other people's houses knows that the best guests are the ones who feel at home and still tidy up.

There are places where this is hard. The picture itself is the first. It is a lord and a servant, a medieval picture, and some readers will hear only the ranks in it and not like them. What Julian takes from it is the stooping, not the ranking. The servant is not honoured by being told where he stands, but by being met.

The second hard place is that you may not feel it. Some days the road is not courteous at all. A shop is shut when you need it. A path has been churned to mud. A face you needed to be kind is not. Julian is not describing the courtesy of the world. She is also careful to say that this was her sight, and she wrote
as to my sight
often enough that it is hard to miss: she is telling you what she saw, not telling you what you must feel.

And there is a question under the whole picture, which is whether you can be that kind of person yourself. It would be a poor reading of the passage that stopped at being on the receiving end. If the greatest thing a lord can do is to be homely and glad of heart, then the same is true at every level. Courtesy is one of the few things a tired walker can still give away.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? A small, steady politeness. A first greeting, before the other person has made theirs. A thank-you that is said looking at the person. A name remembered. A room left a little better than you found it. And, now and then, the nerve to be at ease: to accept the bowl, to sit at the table, to let someone be glad to have you.
For the walk

items.t: Who has been homely with me in the last day, treating me as one of the house, and did I notice at the time?
Be courteous on purpose, once, to someone who will never know it was on purpose. Say good morning first, or
buen Camino
if there is someone to say it to. Look at the person as you do. And if no one is there, say a thank you to the road, aloud, in a plain voice.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A shared table is a great leveller. Whatever you were at breakfast, tonight you are someone with a fork and a plate, in a room with a few others who have also come a long way. If you are in a village where you are the only walker, the table may be for one, and the kindness may only be a nod across a counter. That counts. Think about the people who made the room you are sitting in, and what they must have done to have it ready for a stranger.

Run through the day and find the stoopings. Who bent down to your level? It might have been a person with a hose and a smile, or a message that came at just the right time, or a fellow walker who slowed down a little so that you did not have to ask. Some of these will be so small that you have to look twice. They were still a lord being homely.

Then turn the question round. Where did you do it for someone else? And where did you hold back, from tiredness or irritation or plain forgetfulness? Courtesy is the first thing to go at the end of a hard day, and the last thing anyone remembers. If you were short with someone, a sentence tomorrow morning will mend more than a long apology tonight.

Be fair to yourself as well. Julian's two words, homely and courteous, hold something you can turn on your own tired self. Be at home in your own skin tonight, and be gentle with it. A walker who has been sharp with their own feet all day has not been courteous to the person who carried them.
If none of this came to mind, that is also an answer. Some days are plain, and a plain day can still end with a clean bed.

items.t: Who made me feel at home today, and what did they actually do?
Where was I short on courtesy, with someone else or with myself?
Whom could I be homely with tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for every door that opened today. Thank you for the hands that made the beds. Teach me the manners of someone who is glad. Let me be at home where I am a guest, and kind where I am the stranger. Bless the house I sleep in, and whoever keeps it.
What do you do with a question that has no answer yet?
The passage

paras.t: But in this I stood beholding things general, troublously and mourning, saying thus to our Lord in my meaning, with full great dread:
Ah! good Lord, how might all be well, for the great hurt that is come, by sin, to the creature?

And here I desired, as far as I durst, to have some more open declaring wherewith I might be eased in this matter. … Another understanding is this, that there be deeds evil done in our sight, and so great harms taken, that it seemeth to us that it were impossible that ever it should come to good end. And upon this we look, sorrowing and mourning therefor, so that we cannot resign us unto the blissful beholding of God as we should do. And the cause of this is that the use of our reason is now so blind, so low, and so simple, that we cannot know that high marvellous Wisdom, the Might and the Goodness of the blissful Trinity.

spans.t: Reflection

There is a kind of morning when the sky is clear, the path is dry, the birds are going about their business, and you are carrying something that none of it touches. A message from home. A diagnosis. A name that comes into the mind and will not leave. The road is lovely and the heart is somewhere else. You may be walking beside the most beautiful scenery in Spain and feel nothing, and then feel guilty for feeling nothing.
Julian knew that morning. This is the day to say so plainly, because if the book were to hurry past it, it would not be worth carrying.

Here is where she stands in the book. She has just been told, in words she will make famous, that all shall be well. We will come to that tomorrow. But she does not leave the matter there, and she does not nod and move on. She stands, in her words,
beholding things general, troublously and mourning
, and she asks the question that is in the back of almost every mind: how can it be? Look at the great hurt that has come into the world. How could all be well?
Notice that she dares to ask. She says she desired an answer
as far as I durst
, which is an honest little phrase: she wanted more than she thought she was allowed to want. And she puts the question in the plainest language she has.

Then she says something even more candid, in the second part. There are deeds evil done in our sight, and harms so great, that it seems impossible they could ever come to a good end. And when we look at them, we sorrow so much that we cannot settle ourselves to look at God. She makes no attempt to wave that away. She does not call the harms small, or say that they only seem bad. She calls them great and she says the sorrow they cause is real enough to block the view.

What she offers instead of an answer is an admission of limits. The cause of our not knowing, she says, is that our reason is so blind, so low and so simple that it cannot take in the Wisdom, Might and Goodness she is talking about. That is not an explanation of suffering. It is a confession that she does not have one. In the chapter's own terms, the answer exists, and it is hidden.
A word about "sin", since it is her word. We tend to hear it as private guilt. Julian does not mean only that. When she writes the word, she says in chapter 27, it brought to her mind
all that is not good

, and the pains of every creature, bodily and spiritual. She is looking at the whole sorrow of the world, and her own small part in it. She lived through hard times. The introduction to the edition speaks of plague, riot and war in her century, and a sensible reader will not be surprised that her question is not an idle one.
There are harder sayings in these chapters, and it would be dishonest to pretend that there are not. She writes in chapter 27 that pain, as she sees it, serves a purpose for a time,
for it purgeth

. It is a thing to say to oneself, if one says it at all, and never to someone else in pain. In chapter 32 she turns to what her Church taught about those who are lost, and says that it seemed to her impossible that all could be well. We do not follow her down that road in this book. It is there in the text, and she does not hide it.

What does this ask of an ordinary day? First, permission. You are allowed to carry a question that has no answer, and to say so, and you are not obliged to dress it up as faith or as despair. Second, a little company for it. She says in chapter 28 that
each kind compassion that man hath on his even-Christians with charity, it is Christ in him

. Her word is fellow-Christians, and you may stretch it as far as it will go. The thing it describes is simple. When you feel for another person's hurt and do something kind about it, that is as much as anyone can ask.
If you can do nothing at all today, and the question stays the size it was at breakfast, walk anyway. The question can walk with you.
For the walk

items.t: If I dared, as Julian dared, what would I ask this morning?

Say that question once, aloud, under your breath if there is someone near. Do not answer it. Then walk for ten minutes noticing only what is in front of you: the sound of your boots, the colour of a wall. If a kind thought about someone else comes, follow it a little way.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Some days have no neat shape. Today may be one of them. You may have carried something heavy from breakfast to dusk and set it down in the same place you picked it up, no lighter and no clearer. Nothing here is going to tell you that this was wrong.

If it was a heavy day, say what it was heavy with. It need not be a sentence for anyone else. A name, or a word, or the sound of a phone not ringing. It helps, sometimes, to hear it in your own voice, in the dark, with nobody to correct it. Julian did exactly this. She said it to the One she was talking to, and she said it without an apology.

Then look for the other thing. Even on the worst days there are usually moments of kindness, and they are easy to miss when you are looking for something else. A hand held out over a stile. A woman who asked how far you had come, and waited for the answer. A sentence in a text. These do not prove that all is well. They are not meant to. They are what a little compassion looks like when it is in the room.

If you are tired as well as heavy, put the heaviness down for the night, as you would put down the pack. It will be there in the morning, and so will you, and it is not a failure of love to sleep. You have not stopped caring for the thing by letting it rest.

If there is someone who could carry it with you for an hour, a friend, a priest, a stranger at the next table, the evening is a good time to think about asking. Julian never claims that the great hurt is borne alone.

items.t: What did I carry today that I could not mend?
Where did I see, or do, something kind, however small?
Who might I let carry this with me, even for an hour?

spans.t: A short prayer

I have a question, and tonight there is no answer. Hear it anyway. Be with whoever is hurting, near or far, and with me. Let me be kind where I can. Let the dark be gentle, and the morning not too sudden.
Can a promise made without a plan still be kept?
The passage

paras.t: But Jesus, who in this Vision informed me of all that is needful to me, answered by this word and said:
It behoved that there should be sin; … but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
… These words were said full tenderly, showing no manner of blame to me nor to any that shall be saved. …
I may make all thing well, I can make all thing well, I will make all thing well, and I shall make all thing well; and thou shalt see thyself that all manner of thing shall be well.

… He willeth we know that not only He taketh heed to noble things and to great, but also to little and to small, to low and to simple, to one and to other. And so meaneth He in that He saith: ALL MANNER OF THINGS
shall be well
. For He willeth we know that the least thing shall not be forgotten.

spans.t: Reflection

By now you may have seen the sentence on a mug. It turns up on tea towels and cards and the walls of waiting rooms, in a nice typeface, and it has the problem of anything repeated too often. Read on a mug, "all shall be well" sounds like advice to cheer up. You would not say it to a friend whose house had burned down, and you would be right.

So it is worth knowing where it comes from. Julian did not pick it up in passing. It was given to her in the middle of her own distress, after she had long wondered why the world should hold so much hurt, and had mourned over it. And the words come
full tenderly, showing no manner of blame
: no scolding in them, no impatience with her for asking. The first thing the sentence does is to let her off being told off.

Notice the order in her book, too. The promise is in chapter 27. The question we read yesterday comes two chapters later, in chapter 29. She was told, and she still asked. Being given a sentence did not end her wondering, and nothing here suggests that it should end yours.

Now look at how the promise is built. When it comes again, in chapter 31, it is four short clauses in a row, each opening with a different verb: may, can, will, shall. Able, skilled, willing, certain. It is the shape of a promise from someone who has thought of every excuse you might make. Is it in his power? Yes. Does he know how? Yes. Does he want to? Yes. Then he shall.
Next, look at
all manner of thing
. Julian herself spells out what that includes. God, she writes, takes heed not only to the great and the noble, but
to little and to small, to low and to simple

. And so the least thing shall not be forgotten. This is the hazelnut again, from the first day. The promise is not about the great matters only. It covers the blister, the lost glove, the afternoon that went wrong, and the person nobody noticed in the corner. If the whole world is the size of a nut, the smallest thing in it has a place.
Now for what makes this hard. The first thing is the clause that most readers wish had been left out.
It behoved that there should be sin.
She does not explain it, and she does not claim to. Elsewhere, in chapter 35, she draws a line between what God does and what God lets happen:
all that is good our Lord doeth, and that which is evil our Lord suffereth

. She adds at once that she does not call any evil worshipful. She is not excusing the harm. She is saying that it is not the last word, and that she cannot see how. If you find that sentence hard to read, you are in good company, and Julian is one of the company.
The second hard thing is the tense. It says
shall
. It does not say
is
. Tonight's sore feet, and the person you are grieving, are not made well by the promise on any day that you can see. The how is hidden, too: of the way it will be done she writes in chapter 32 that
How it shall be done there is no creature beneath Christ that knoweth it
. A promise with no plan attached is a thing that can only be taken on trust.

The third is how easily the sentence can be used badly. "It will all be fine" is what one person says to another when they have run out of attention. Julian's sentence is not that. It was given to her in her own sorrow, and she carried it for the rest of her life before she handed it on. If you ever offer it to someone else, you may want to do it much more quietly than a mug would.

So what does it ask of an ordinary day? Something like what the road already asks. You walk on a map and a sentence. You do not see the end. You trust that the next waymark will be where the last one said, and mostly it is. This sentence asks for the same sort of trust, with a larger destination, and it does not ask you to feel any particular way about it. Hold it as a promise and not as a prediction. A prediction can be checked this evening. A promise is a thing you lean on.
If it helps, try it to the rhythm of your steps. There are five syllables in the middle of it, and it fits a breath. If it jars, leave it alone. It will keep.
For the walk

items.t: Which small thing that I have dismissed as too minor to matter is one of the all manner of things?

Walk for ten minutes with one of the four verbs from the passage: may, can, will, shall. Pick the one you most need today, and let it keep time with your feet. Say nothing else, and see which one you reach for tomorrow.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The light goes in stages at this time of day. The sky holds on to its colour for a while after the ground has given it up. If you can see a window from where you are sitting, you may find that it has turned from blue to grey while you were not looking.

You have walked a day with a sentence in your pocket. How did it fare? Some hours it will have rung hollow, and you will have been right to let it ring that way. A slogan that survives only in cheerful weather is not worth the keeping. Other hours, perhaps without your noticing, it will have done its small work: a shoulder dropped, a grip loosened, a worry set down for an hour. Which was which?

Think about the things today that seemed beyond mending, and look at them from here. Some will have mended themselves, or been mended by a meal and a wash. One or two will not have. They are still there, and there is no shame in that. A promise is not a bandage that sticks on the same afternoon.

Think also about who needs company tonight rather than advice. If someone you love is carrying a hurt, the kindest use of Julian's sentence may be to say none of it, and sit there. It was given to her in her own sorrow. It does not follow that it is yours to hand to someone in theirs.
An honest word about tiredness: a promise is not an instruction to be cheerful. You are allowed to be flat. Being flat is not a failure to believe; it is being tired.

items.t: Where did it feel today as though nothing could be well, and how did that feeling stand by evening?
Which small thing from today do I want to remember?
Who needs my company tonight more than my advice?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I leave the big things where they are. Let the small ones be remembered. Keep what I cannot fix, and mend what I cannot see. Give me trust enough for the morning. Let all that I love be held, and let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 6. Prayer that tastes of nothing

spans.t: Does it count when it feels like nothing?
The passage

paras.t: But yet oftentimes our trust is not full: for we are not sure that God heareth us, as we think because of our unworthiness, and because we feel right nought, (for we are as barren and dry oftentimes after our prayers as we were afore); and this, in our feeling our folly, is cause of our weakness. …

I am Ground of thy beseeching: first it is my will that thou have it; and after, I make thee to will it; and after, I make thee to beseech it and thou beseechest it. How should it then be that thou shouldst not have thy beseeching?

Pray inwardly, … though thee thinketh it savour thee not: for it is profitable, though thou feel not, though thou see nought; yea, though thou think thou canst not. For in dryness and in barrenness, in sickness and in feebleness, then is thy prayer well-pleasant to me, though thee thinketh it savour thee nought but little. And so is all thy believing prayer in my sight.

spans.t: Reflection

By the sixth day of a walk, most people have stopped pretending to themselves about at least one thing. Perhaps it is the pace. Perhaps it is the weight of the pack, or the real reason they set out. For some it is also the matter of prayer, or whatever stands in its place: the stillness at the start of the day that you meant to keep and have kept, perhaps, for two mornings. You stand at a gate, the world is quiet, and you feel nothing at all.
If that is where you are, the person who wrote today's passage has been there. Look at how she begins. Our trust is often not full, she says, because we are not sure we are heard, and because we feel
right nought
. We are as barren and dry after our prayers as we were before them. Then, in the very next sentence:
For thus have I felt in myself.
She is not talking about other people. She has been dry herself.
What comes next is the part that has made the chapter loved. She is given a sentence:
I am Ground of thy beseeching.

The wish to pray, the little pull toward stillness that you may be feeling this morning, is not a thing you manufactured. The order she is given is this: first it is God's will that you should have it, then you are made to want it, then you are made to ask for it, and you ask. The asking is the last link in a chain that began somewhere else. The wanting is already part of the answer. And so comes a question that is almost playful, and very tender: how could it be that you should not have what you ask for?

Read plainly, it says that the faintest wish counts. You do not have to feel anything. You do not have to produce a state of mind. Perhaps all you did this morning was look at the sky and want something, without a word for it. That is what she means by
beseeching
, and that is the thing she was shown.
Then the second half is a kind of permission slip. Pray inwardly, she says,
though thee thinketh it savour thee not

: though it tastes of nothing. It is profitable though you feel nothing, see nothing, and think you cannot. In dryness and barrenness, in sickness and feebleness, that is when your prayer is well-pleasing. She is not saying this to people who feel fine. She is saying it to people who are dry, ill and weak, and she means them to hear it as welcome.

For a walker there is something close to home here. A long road has its own dry places: chapped lips, a throat that wants water, a patience worn thin. A prayer that tastes of nothing is not a failure of the prayer. It is what one would expect in a tired and weathered creature on a long road. She does not say that walking is prayer. She says that dry, unfelt attention is welcome, and what counts as that, for you, is for you to say.

Now the hard places. The first is a simple one: all this assumes that someone is on the other end, and if you are not sure of that, the passage does not make it so. You can still take the human part from it. Wanting counts. A faint turning toward what you need is real, whether or not you have a name for what it turns to.
The second is harder.
How should it then be that thou shouldst not have thy beseeching?

There are people who have asked, with their whole hearts, for something that did not come: a recovery, a reconciliation, a life. For them, that question may feel like a slap. Julian saw the difficulty. In the next chapter she writes that when we have prayed a long time and think we have not been given what we asked for, we should not be in heaviness, because
either we abide a better time, or more grace, or a better gift
. It may not satisfy you. It is what she was given, and she passes it on as she received it, without dressing it up.
What does it ask of an ordinary day? Less than you might think. The smallest possible prayer: a breath, a name, a word like
here
. And the willingness to leave it without feedback. The door of a locked church, a gate in a wall, a quiet bit of path: any of these is enough. You do not have to feel that it worked.
For the walk

items.t: If the wish to pray, or just to be still, is itself a gift, what is it asking for right now?
At the next gate, wall or milestone, stop for one minute with no words. If you want one, use a single word,
here
, on the out-breath. If nothing comes, count the minute as done and walk on. It counts either way.

spans.t: At the end of the day

It is easy to fall asleep in the middle of a prayer. It is an old joke, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. A tired body prays badly, and the passage names feebleness as one of the times when prayer is well-pleasing. If the first thing you do tonight is yawn, you have started well.

Go back through the day and look for the moments that were closest to praying, without being called that. It may have been the first sight of a valley opening out. It may have been a half-minute of complete quiet in a doorway. It may have been an irritation turned into a plea: please, let this hill end. These are not nothing. They are the same wanting that Julian is talking about, in work clothes.

Then look at the dry stretches, the hours where you felt nothing at all. Today may have been mostly one long dry stretch. Say so, and be honest about it. The passage does not ask you to be grateful for the dryness. It says that dry prayer is welcome
in dryness and in barrenness
, not instead of it. You are allowed to wish it had been otherwise.

If you are carrying a request that has not been answered, the evening can be a very quiet time for it. You need not argue with it or give it up. Julian's own words are that the answer may be a better time, or more grace, or a better gift, and she leaves it open which. You do not have to choose tonight.
Prayer, at the end of a day like this, can be very small. The whole of it may be the word you whispered at the gate this morning, said once more with your eyes closed.

items.t: What did I want today, underneath everything else I wanted?
Where did I feel nothing, and could I let that be enough?
Is there a request I am carrying that I could hold more loosely tonight?

spans.t: A short prayer
Here I am, and I have little to say. Take the wish for the words. Take the dry hours with the rest. Be near whoever I cannot help. Let me sleep inside whatever I could not pray.

chapters.title: Day 7. A light for the night

spans.t: How much of the road do you need to see?
The passage

paras.t: Our faith is a light by nature coming of our endless Day, that is our Father, God. In which light our Mother, Christ, and our good Lord, the Holy Ghost, leadeth us in this passing life. This light is measured discreetly, needfully standing to us in the night. … For we, with mercy and grace, steadfastly know and believe our light, going therein wisely and mightily. And at the end of woe, suddenly our eyes shall be opened, and in clearness of light our sight shall be full: which light is God, our Maker and Holy Ghost, in Christ Jesus our Saviour. Thus I saw and understood that our faith is our light in our night: which light is God, our endless Day.

spans.t: Reflection

If you ever set out in the dark with a head torch, you know the small round room of light it makes. A few paces of path, a patch of grass, a stone that you would otherwise have turned your ankle on. Beyond it, nothing. Behind it, nothing. Yet you walk, and the room walks with you, and the path turns out to be there, one lit stretch after another.
It is a strange way to cross a country, and it is how most of a long road is crossed. You are never shown the whole of it. You are shown enough.
Julian reaches for the same picture near the end of her book, though she does it with faith and not with a battery. Our faith, she says, is a light that comes
of our endless Day
: the sun, as it were, from the other side of the hill, throwing a first grey up the sky before you can see it. And this light, she adds, is
measured discreetly, needfully standing to us in the night
. Measured: given out in the right amount. Discreetly: with judgement, not wastefully, not stingily. Standing to us: set down where we need it, like a lamp on a table in a dark house.
A little further on she is more exact still.
Neither is the light so large that we may see our blissful Day, nor is it shut from us.
That sentence is the one to carry. The light is not so large that you can see the end. Nor is it shut: you are not left in the dark. What you get is neither the whole view nor nothing. It is a lamp.

That is a hard thing to be told on the seventh day. The novelty has gone. The finish is not in sight. You may have a long middle to walk, with the road looking much as it did yesterday and the day before. This is where patience comes in. Julian knew about long patience. The showings that came to her took a few hours of one morning, and she spent the rest of her life trying to understand them. She says herself that
fifteen years after, and more
she was given the meaning. In chapter 64 she writes that a person
lengtheneth his patience over the time of his living
. The word she chooses is "lengtheneth": patience that is stretched, as a road is stretched, over distance.
Now to the hard places. First, a sentence we left out. Between the two parts of the passage, Julian says that the light is the cause of our life, and the night is the cause of our pain and our woe,
in which we earn meed and thanks of God

. "Meed" is an old word for reward. It is her medieval way of saying that the night is not wasted, and it is hard to hear if the night is only night to you, a grief with no reward in sight. We have left it between the two parts for you to find in the book if you want it. Nothing in the rest of today's passage depends on it.

The second is the word "faith". If you are walking without it, the light in this passage may seem to describe something you do not have. Take whatever light you do have, the torch, the map, the next arrow, the person ahead of you on the path, and read the picture with that. The shape of it still holds. You are given enough for the next stretch, and no more.
The third is the nights when the light seems too small even for that. Julian does not hide these. In chapter 15 she writes of a time when
there was no comfort nor none ease to me but faith, hope, and charity; and these I had in truth, but little in feeling.
A lamp that is lit and gives hardly any light is still a lamp. It does not feel like one.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? A particular kind of patience: to take the road in the lengths the light allows. Choose a post, a tree, a bend ahead, and walk to it as if it were the whole journey. When you reach it, choose another. This is no trick to get you to the end faster. It is a way of being where you are, in the one room of light that you have, with the whole of the path ahead still hidden and quite likely to be there.
For the walk

items.t: How much of the road do I actually need to see to take the next step?

For ten minutes, walk only to the next thing you can see, a post, a wall, a bend. When you reach it, pick another and let the rest of the road go dark. If your mind runs ahead to the end, bring it back to the lit patch under your feet.

spans.t: At the end of the day

When dusk comes down in a village, the windows come on one at a time, each with its own small yellow room of light. You can tell a good deal about a place from them: where there is a kitchen, where there is a television, where somebody is up late. Each lit window is not much. Together they make a street you could find your way along.

Think of where today's patience held and where it ran out. There is usually a point, mid-afternoon or thereabouts, when it frays: the hill that is longer than the sign said, the path that goes on straight for an hour, the clock that does not move. What did you do when that point came? Did you pick the next marker, or push through it with your jaw set, or sit down? None of these is wrong. Notice only which came naturally.

Think, too, about what you were trying to see the end of. It might be the day. It might be the walk. It might be something quite different, a decision waiting at home, a grief you hoped would be lighter by now, a question about where your life goes next. The light in the passage is measured for the next step, and it does not tell you what the end looks like. That may be a relief or a frustration. Tonight, both are allowed.
If the light today seemed too small, say that without apology. Julian did. A walker who has faith only in the lowest degree, little in feeling, is the very person the sentences were written for.
You may be tired in the particular way of the seventh day, when the body has settled into its rhythm and the mind has run out of novelty. Let the evening be small. A lit window, a warm drink, a bed.

items.t: Where did I want more light today than I was given, and what did the light I had actually show me?
When did my patience run out, and what did it need at that moment?
What am I trying to see the end of, and can I leave it dark for tonight?

spans.t: A short prayer

Give me enough light for the next step. Let me not ask for the whole road tonight. Be patient with me where my patience is thin. Hold the dark ahead, and keep the lamp lit by the bed. In the morning, let there be a little more.
What was begun in you before you took the first step?
The passage

paras.t: Learn it well: Love was His meaning. Who shewed it thee? Love. What shewed He thee? Love. Wherefore shewed it He? For Love. Hold thee therein and thou shalt learn and know more in the same. But thou shalt never know nor learn therein other thing without end.

… And I saw full surely that ere God made us He loved us; which love was never slacked, nor ever shall be. And in this love He hath done all His works; and in this love He hath made all things profitable to us; and in this love our life is everlasting. In our making we had beginning; but the love wherein He made us was in Him from without beginning: in which love we have our beginning. And all this shall we see in God, without end.

spans.t: Reflection

At some point on every long walk there is a morning when you notice that you are close to an ending. It may be today. It may be some days off, with the number of kilometres now small enough to count on the fingers of a few hands. Either way, the feeling starts to turn. For a week the road was a thing you were in. Now it is becoming a thing you will have done.
Julian was at that point when she wrote the chapter we have been reading from. It is the last chapter of her book. And the first thing she says in it is not "this is done" but the opposite:
This book is begun by God's gift and His grace, but it is not yet performed, as to my sight.
The book finishes by saying that it is not finished. It is worth reading that again slowly, standing up, perhaps with your hand on a gate.

Then she goes back to the question she had been carrying for fifteen years and more. What was it for? What did it all mean? And she is answered, as she says, in her understanding, with a little catechism of five lines. What did he mean? Love. Who showed it to you? Love. What did he show you? Love. Why did he show it? For love. And then the instruction: hold yourself in that, and you shall learn and know more in the same. But you shall never learn anything else, in it, without end.

You can hear how plain it is. After all the visions, the sights of suffering and glory, the long wrestling with sin and pain, the whole thing comes down to a sentence a child could say. And she says it took fifteen years and more to be given it. It is not an answer to be hurried to.

The second half of the passage turns to beginnings. Before God made us, she writes, He loved us, and that love was never slackened and never will be. In our making we had beginning; but the love in which we were made was in Him from without beginning. And
in which love we have our beginning

Think what that does to the idea of an ending. If the love you were made in came before your beginning, then there was no first step, in the deepest sense. You did not start this walk from nothing. Whatever it was that turned you towards the road, a grief, a restlessness, a curiosity, a wish for quiet, had already begun in you, and had a history longer than your wish to walk. You did not start the Camino. It found you in the middle of something that was already going on.
There are hard places in the passage, and the end of a book is a fair place to say them. The first is
never know nor learn therein other thing without end

. To a seeker, that can sound like a door closing. Is there to be no more explanation? She does not apologise. She is not saying that nothing else can be learned. She is saying that nothing deeper can be, and that is a different claim, though it is hard to feel on a day when you want to understand why a particular thing happened.

The second is that love as the meaning of everything does not explain the hurt. It is not an argument. It does not account for plague, or a death, or the weather of a bad year. Read after the other days, it is not trying to. It comes at the end of a book that has looked at the hurt without flinching, and it comes after fifteen years, not fifteen minutes. If it sounds too easy, it does not come from ease.

A third is more personal. You may not have found any such meaning in your own walk. It may have been plain walking: feet, weather, sleep. That is a respectable thing to have found. The five questions are Julian's, about Julian's showings. You do not have to answer them with her answer. You may answer
I don't know yet
, and she would understand: she waited fifteen years.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Perhaps just a different relation to the ending. Not "I have finished", but "I have been begun". A road is not used up when you reach the end of it. In another place she writes that God shewed Himself in the earth
thus as it were in pilgrimage
, here with us, leading us. If that is so, then the leading does not stop at the last yellow arrow.
For the walk

items.t: If a child asked me why I am here, who or what set me on this road, what has it shown me, and why did I come, what would I say in one word each?

Take the three questions, Who, What, Wherefore, and put them to the road. Let each answer be a single word, and do not look for a clever one. Say them to the next three markers you pass, one word each, and see if the words keep.

spans.t: At the end of the day

This is the last evening of the book. It may or may not be the last evening of your walk. Either way, a certain tenderness is permitted. Eight days ago you opened a small thing, and it may have grown a little, in the way that a good companion does, without ever being much trouble.

Look back not just over today but over the eight days. The first day was a nut in a palm. Then a layer of cloth, a door that opened, a hurt that did not have an answer, a sentence on a mug that turned out to have a history. Then a dry prayer, and a little light for a dark morning. If you were to pick one of them to keep, which would it be? It need not be the one you expected. A person can walk a long way for the sake of one image.

Be honest about what did not land. Some days will have been flat. Some passages will have asked for a belief that you do not hold, or a trust that you did not have to give. That is not a failure of the road or the book. Take what helped and leave the rest in the bunk.

And look at the question of the beginning once more. When did this start? Not the day you booked, or the day you set out, but the first moment you wanted something like this. Where was it, and what was it wanting? You might find that the walk is the reply to something older than the walk.
You are allowed to be tired and to be done. An ending is a little like going out of a lit room into a dark yard. There is a moment of nothing, and then the eyes adjust and there are stars.

items.t: What from these eight days do I want to keep?
What was already begun in me before I set out?
Where will I begin again tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the road, and for what began before it. Let me carry the little I have understood, and not be afraid of the rest. Let the ending be a beginning. Keep what I have loved. Be with me tomorrow, wherever the first step falls.

You have come to the end of the eight days, or you are stopping early, or you mean to go back to a day that you skipped. Any of these is fine. The book is not a course, and nobody is marking it. It was made to be a little company on a quiet road, and company does not have to stay once the road is done.
Eight small things
You cannot take the whole book with you, and you should not try. But eight small things fit in a pocket, and each of them is something you have already held once.

items.t: The hazelnut: made, loved, kept.
The layers: cloth, skin, flesh, bone, heart, and something around all of them that does not wear out.
The open door: homely and courteous together, being welcomed and welcoming.
The question without an answer, which is allowed to walk beside you.
The promise without a plan: that nothing, down to the least thing, is forgotten.
The prayer that tastes of nothing, and counts.
The lamp that shows the next step, and no more.
The beginning that came before the first step.

spans.t: Pick one. Not the best one, the one that cost you least and gave you most. You can do without the others for a while.
Going on

If you would like more of Julian, she is easy to find. The edition we have used, from 1901, is free at Project Gutenberg as ebook number 52958, and it is the same text every passage here was checked against. Her chapters are short, and the book can be read a chapter at a time, as it was once read by people with a long day ahead of them. You will find our eight days in chapters 5 to 7 and 77, 27 to 32, 41 and 83 to 86. The editor's long introduction is not needed, and you can skip it.

A warning is fair. Much of the book is about the suffering of Christ, seen in visions she describes without softening. We have left those chapters aside. They are hers, and they will mean most to readers who share her faith. If you read on, read what helps, and pass quietly over what does not.

Be honest, too, about what did not work. A day that left you cold on the road may speak to you in a kitchen in March. A passage that asked for more belief than you had is not a test you failed. The book is not a test. If something hardly touched you, nothing has gone wrong.
A last word

Julian spent her life, as far as we know, in a small room beside a church, with a window onto the services and a window onto the street. It is hard to think of a life with less road in it. Yet in chapter 81 she writes that God shewed Himself in the earth
thus as it were in pilgrimage
, here with us, leading us, until we are brought to the end. She did not need to walk to know what a walker knows: that the going is the thing, and that someone is in it.

If you remember only one sentence, the one she was given is short enough. It is all right to say it quietly, to nobody in particular, on an ordinary afternoon with the road in front of you and no sight of the end:
all manner of thing shall be well.
Walk again, when you can. Or tomorrow, round the block, with your phone left behind and your hands open.
Buen Camino.
